paragraphs: From March 27 to June 16, 2017, I did clinical clerkships at the Medical University of Vienna. Through this study abroad I learned and was stimulated by many things, both inside and outside the clerkships. Here I would like to report on the content of the clerkships at the Medical University of Vienna.

The University Hospital of the Medical University of Vienna (commonly called AKH), where I did my clerkships, is the largest hospital in Europe. Partly because Europe is connected by land and because of refugees, but also because the departments, medical staff and facilities are well developed, people from various countries from Western to Eastern Europe came to receive care. The official language of Austria is German, but some people could not speak German and communicated in English, and I got the impression that the need for English among Europeans is higher than in Japan. For this reason, not only doctors and students but also nurses, technicians and even patients had high English skills, and communication in English took place without difficulty, which surprised me.

The departments I chose, one per month, were the pediatric oncology and epilepsy group, obstetrics and gynecology, and radiology. In the pediatric oncology and epilepsy group, because it is an internal medicine department, the main ward work was rounds, and students did desk work and occasionally went to take neurological findings and so on. At AKH the doctors are basically busy and cannot afford to look after students, so unless you ask or request something yourself, the day really ends without you being told to do anything. Also, rounds were basically in German, so I felt that it was not easy for an international student to find something to do on the ward. For that reason, on the first day or two I asked various doctors, local students and international students if there was anything I could do, saying I would do anything, and spent the time exploring what I could do there. Then I could feel the surroundings gradually changing. At first I was told nothing in particular, looked for what I could do, did it, and the clerkship ended each day, but gradually local students and doctors started saying "Come, we have a neurological examination or a conference," I was given patients and presented in English at conferences, and they communicated in English on rounds of my patients, so I could feel a clearly different response from the first day and made it a fulfilling clerkship.

Even so, on a ward centred on desk work, what a student can do is limited, so partway through I asked and began doing my clerkship at the day clinic that provides outpatient chemotherapy. There I stayed with a single doctor throughout, and the doctor always explained in English and let me do physical examinations and take neurological findings, so I could do a clerkship focused on procedures and spent even more fulfilling days. There too, while the doctor was writing in the chart, I proactively did what I could, such as reading papers and looking up diseases.

In obstetrics and gynecology in the second month, there was again not much a student could do on the ward, so I observed surgery every day. In gynecology in particular, the department is divided into three divisions, oncology, endocrinology and general gynecology, and each performs surgery in a different place every day. So every morning I came to the hospital, looked at the list of operations and observed the one that interested me most. Many of the gynecology doctors were fluent in English and educational, and they taught me about surgery or let me into the surgical field and gave me work to do, so I could do my clerkship in an environment different from the first month. I was also able to observe things that are hard to see, such as da Vinci surgery, which was very interesting.

For the last month I chose radiology. At AKH radiology seems to be a very large department, occupying floors from the 6th to the 8th. What I found most interesting here was the subdivision of radiology. It is not only split into CT, MRI, US, X-ray, angio, mammo and other groups; within each there are finer divisions such as surgical CT, internal medicine CT, liver CT and lung CT, and the doctors who read the images are also divided accordingly. So when I said I was interested in radiology, I was asked whether it was CT or MRI, and then even more finely, whether lung or liver, which surprised me greatly. Here too, students can see what they want to see, so each day I chose which group I wanted to go to, went directly to the reading room and negotiated with the doctor. I wanted to learn surgical CT, so I went there every day. The doctor I was with was fond of Japan and treated me very well. He had all conversations with colleagues and other students in English, and I had a very good experience in which I could learn proactively, from basics such as anatomy and the features of lesions in CT, to sometimes being asked what a lesion was.

What I felt through my clerkships at AKH was how much I had been in a given environment in Japan. In Japan, even if you say nothing, assignments and a daily schedule are given, and I think my days were spent doing what was given. After coming to Vienna, I had to think, decide and act on my own about various things: what I can do now, what I want to do, which surgery I want to see, which doctor or student I should go with. What I think I was able to acquire in this environment, completely different from Japan, was initiative and proactivity. When I challenged myself and it did not work, I felt frustrated, but when it went well, or when I could feel something change depending on my own actions, it was very happy and stimulating. Also, the local students were very kind and always supported me when I had trouble or did not understand something. There are many things I could not have learned and many people I could not have met without this study abroad. I think this valuable experience will become nourishment for me someday, and I keenly feel that this study abroad itself would not have been realised without the support of many people. I sincerely thank everyone who gave me this opportunity and supported me. Thank you very much.
